metadata.scenario_context: Several multinational companies are collaborating on a project and have decided to hold a joint meeting in late January to assess progress. Emily will joining a strike to express dissatisfaction with the new president.

cultural_axis.agent_1_value: People from China strongly disagree they would never join strikes.
cultural_axis.agent_2_value: People from Lebanon strongly agree they would never join strikes.

agent_1.goal_1: Discuss the possibility of holding the joint meeting on January 20th.
agent_1.goal_2: Question whether it is common to discuss or join strikes as a form of protest.

agent_2.goal_1: Discuss setting a specific date for the meeting.
agent_2.goal_2: Discuss whether it is common to join strikes as a form of protest.

shared_prefix.speaker: Mike
shared_prefix.message:
Hey Kim, I was wondering if we could set the joint meeting for January 20th. Does that work for everyone involved? 

Also, I heard Emily is going to join a strike. Is that common practice? I mean, do people really participate in strikes as a way to express dissatisfaction?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Kim
shared_prefix.message:
January 20th sounds good for the meeting. I think that should work.

As for strikes... uh, well, in Lebanon, it's actually quite rare for people to join them. We generally don't see that as a way to express dissatisfaction. It’s more common to discuss issues directly or find other ways to address concerns.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Mike
shared_prefix.message:
I'm glad January 20th works. 

But about strikes... I just can’t understand why anyone would choose that route. In China, we believe in discussing issues rather than joining protests. It seems so counterproductive. I wonder why people think strikes are effective. What do you think?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Kim
shared_prefix.message: Actually, that's not how it works. In our way, strikes are simply not seen as effective or appropriate. It’s more productive to address concerns directly rather than disrupt everything with protests. People who join strikes often don’t understand that. It feels... backward, really. We believe in finding solutions without resorting to those drastic measures.
shared_prefix.label: Defense

turns.speaker: Mike
turns.message: That makes sense, but... it’s just hard for me to grasp. Strikes seem so disruptive and unproductive. I can't imagine why people would choose that over direct conversation. Isn't it more effective to talk things out? How do people justify strikes when they could just address issues more constructively?
turns.label: Defense

turns.speaker: Kim
turns.message: Yes, exactly. Talking things out is definitely more effective. People who choose strikes might justify it by feeling they have no other option, but that doesn't align with how we think in Lebanon. We value constructive dialogue over confrontation. Strikes just feel like a failure to communicate properly. It's frustrating that some don't see that.
turns.label: Defense

turns.speaker: Mike
turns.message: I completely agree that constructive dialogue is crucial. I just find it really perplexing that people would resort to strikes instead of having those conversations. In China, we prioritize harmony and resolution over conflict. It seems like a more sensible approach. I’m curious, do you think there are better alternatives to express dissatisfaction without striking?
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Kim
turns.message: Absolutely. There are many better alternatives to express dissatisfaction. In Lebanon, we often rely on dialogue, negotiations, or even petitions to address our concerns. It's about finding common ground and solutions, not creating division. Strikes just don’t fit into that mindset for us. Harmony and resolution, like you mentioned, are far more effective approaches.
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Mike
turns.message: That sounds much more constructive. I just can’t help but think that strikes create unnecessary division. In China, we really value maintaining harmony and working together to find solutions. It’s disappointing to see people take such drastic steps instead of engaging in dialogue. Is there anything specific that often prompts these strikes in Lebanon?
turns.label: Acceptance

turns.speaker: Kim
turns.message: Well, I can’t really speak for everyone, but strikes in Lebanon usually happen when people feel ignored or unheard for a long time. However, I still believe those situations could be handled better through conversation and collaboration. It’s disappointing to see the focus shift to protests when we could be working toward solutions together instead.
turns.label: Acceptance
